title: The one question to ask mini-whiteboard sceptics
author: Craig Barton
summary: Craig Barton argues that the standard objections to mini-whiteboards (cost, handing out and collecting, misuse) are best answered not with tips but with one question: if you will not use them, how will you get an accurate sense of effort and understanding from every student? He then runs through the five replies he hears: Cold Call, circulating, multiple-choice diagnostic questions, technology, and simply knowing the students. Each is dismissed as sampling too few students, taking too long, being inflexible, adding faff and cost, or relying on guesswork instead of evidence. Once teachers accept that whole-class evidence is worth having, the practical barriers become problems to overcome rather than reasons not to try. He is candid that the case is strongest in maths and points to colleagues who show whiteboards working in other subjects.
points: Reframing the debate from the hassle of whiteboards to the need for evidence from every student moves sceptics to a different question.

Each of the five common alternatives has a specific weakness, from small samples in Cold Call to circulation blackspots, pre-prepared multiple-choice items, the faff of technology, and well-informed guesswork.
Barton still pairs whiteboards with Cold Call for long answers, multiple choice for finite answers, and circulation for effort.
He limits his claim to maths and points to science, English, economics and history practitioners for evidence in other subjects.
quotes: If you are not going to use mini-whiteboards, how are you going to get an accurate sense of the effort and understanding of every student?

But the problem with Cold Call is that you only hear from one or two students per answer. Of course, you can be tactical in which students you choose, but you still risk making assumptions about whole-class understanding based on a very small sample of data.
Walking around the classroom is probably the most effective way to get a sense of every student’s level of effort and understanding, but it is certainly not the most efficient.
But the problem with multiple-chocie questions is the answer is one of the options. Therefore, it does not need to be generated by the student.

Technology can be great, but the faff-factor is likely to be significantly more than with a mini-whiteboard in terms of giving out the equipment, students logging in, making sure it is charged, and so on.

Great teachers know their students well and may be able to predict with good accuracy who will understand something and who will not, and who will put in the effort and who will not. But we can all be surprised sometimes, and I would take concrete evidence of effort and understanding over well-informed guesswork any day of the week.
But as a maths teacher, I cannot think of a lesson that would be as effective without each student having access to a mini-whiteboard.
